prompt.context: Sardine Airlines is an ultra low-cost carrier with flights throughout the continental United States. They have hub airports in Oakland, California; Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Hartford, Connecticut. Sardine Airlines is facing increased pressure from other low cost carriers such as Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines. Sardine Airlines has faced declining profit for the past year.
prompt.question: Sardine's CEO, Penny McPincher, has asked your team for advice on how to reverse the profitability trend. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines competes primarily on having the lowest cost fares and offering minimal service. Due to its business model, Sardine has a culture of cost savings that can be passed to the customer.

clarifying_info.q: What is the target profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines is trying to grow profit margin to 20% (net income / total revenue).

clarifying_info.q: Can I see revenue and cost data?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — here is Exhibit 1, the Statement of Operations.
Non-ticket revenue includes bag fees, food, beverages, customer service charges, paper tickets, etc.
Landing fees are what Sardine Airlines pays to use airports.

exhibits.title: Statement of Operations
exhibits.shows: Income statement for Sardine Airlines from 2012 to 2015 showing passenger revenue, non-ticket revenue, total revenue, and operating expenses broken down by fuel, landing fees, maintenance, SG&A, and special charges, leading to net income.

exhibits.title: SG&A Breakdown
exhibits.shows: Bar chart breaking down SG&A expenses for 2014 and 2015 into five categories: Salaries, Marketing, Rent, Customer Service, and Miscellaneous, with dollar amounts in millions for each category and year.

exhibits.title: FAA Memorandum — Sardine Maintenance Record
exhibits.shows: A memorandum from Michael Huerta, Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), to Penny McPincher, CEO of Sardine Airlines, dated June 30, 2015, regarding Sardine Airlines' maintenance record and FAA oversight status.

data.subject: Sardine Airlines Maintenance Record
key_statements: Sardine Airlines is no longer under maintenance supervision from the FAA as of today
The FAA believes the improved maintenance program no longer warrants FAA intervention
Any future decrease in maintenance standards will result in FAA supervision or sanctions

framework: Diagnose revenue trends: assess passenger and non-ticket revenue growth year-over-year to determine if revenue is driving the decline
Diagnose cost trends: review each cost line as a percent of revenue over time to identify which costs are growing disproportionately
Identify primary profit gap: calculate current profit margin vs. the 20% target to quantify the improvement needed
Prioritize cost drivers: focus on lines where cost as a % of revenue has increased most sharply (SG&A, maintenance)
Develop actionable recommendations: propose specific, feasible cost reductions or revenue enhancements to close the gap
Assess risks: consider one-time costs, operational impact, and regulatory constraints for each lever

questions.prompt: What is Sardine's current profit margin, and how large is the gap to the 20% target?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute 2015 net income margin as 371/2143 = ~17.3%. The 20% target implies net income of 0.20 * 2143 = $428.6M. Gap = $428.6M - $371M = $57.6M additional net income needed. Since taxes are 30%, the pre-tax gap is $57.6M / 0.70 = ~$82.3M, but the casebook focuses on the $57.6M net income gap directly.

math.setup: Current NI margin = Net Income / Total Revenue. Target NI = 20% * Total Revenue. Gap = Target NI - Actual NI.
math.answer: Sardine needs an additional $57.6M in net income to reach a 20% margin.

questions.prompt: What do the revenue trends tell us? Is declining revenue a concern?
questions.guidance: Revenue has continued to grow: total revenue up ~4% YoY in 2015 (2,143 vs. 2,060), 16% in 2014, 13% in 2013. However, passenger revenue was essentially flat (-0.37% YoY). Non-ticket revenue grew 9% YoY. Revenue growth is slowing but not declining. The problem is on the cost side.

math.setup: YoY revenue growth = (Current Year - Prior Year) / Prior Year
math.answer: Revenue is growing slowly; passenger revenue nearly flat. Not the primary driver of declining profit.

questions.prompt: Which cost lines are growing as a proportion of revenue? What is the primary driver of declining profit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute each cost as % of total revenue. SG&A jumped from 15% (2014) to 20% (2015) — an increase of 5 percentage points and the largest single-year proportional jump. Maintenance also rose from 8% to 10%. Fuel has been declining as a % of revenue (efficiency improvement). The primary driver is SG&A. Once identified, the interviewer gives the candidate Exhibit 2.

math.setup: Cost % of revenue = Cost Line / Total Revenue for each year
math.answer: SG&A is the primary driver of declining profit, rising from 15% to 20% of revenue. Maintenance is also rising but secondary.

questions.prompt: What is driving the increase in SG&A? (Exhibit 2 provided)
questions.guidance: Candidate should analyze the YoY change in each SG&A component. Three categories are driving growth meaningfully: Marketing (+$24M, up 52%), Rent (+$40M, up 64%), and Customer Service (+$52M, up 433%). Salaries (+$1M) and Miscellaneous (+$2M) are too small to matter. The total SG&A increase is $119M (428 - 309), and these three categories account for $116M of it.

math.setup: YoY change per SG&A category = 2015 value - 2014 value
steps: Marketing + Rent + Customer Service = 24 + 40 + 52 = +$116M (97% of the increase)
math.answer: Marketing, Rent, and Customer Service collectively explain ~97% of the SG&A increase. These are the three areas to focus on.

questions.prompt: Why is maintenance increasing? (Exhibit 3 provided if candidate raises it)
questions.guidance: The FAA memo reveals that Sardine Airlines had previously been under FAA supervision for inadequate maintenance. The increased spending was necessary to bring maintenance standards to an acceptable level. The candidate should conclude that cutting maintenance is not a viable option — it would risk regulatory sanctions. The client is adamant the maintenance program is running at peak efficiency.

questions.prompt: Given Prompt 2 context (marketing fixed, 12-inch seats causing complaints, rent increase, call center billing spike): what can Sardine do to address these issues?
questions.guidance: Marketing: CEO and Board will not cut marketing — this lever is off the table. Rent: The firm does not need to be headquartered in Oakland, but wants to be near major operations. Tulsa or Hartford rent would be 40% less than current 2015 rent of $86M, saving ~$34.4M. Customer Service: The current call center vendor charges rates ~60% higher because it is US-based with native English speakers. Switching to an overseas vendor could save approximately 60% of 2015 customer service cost. The firm is not interested in increasing seat sizes (actually piloting 8-inch 'steerage' seats). Candidate should recommend HQ relocation and vendor switch, and caution against further reducing seat size.

math.setup: Rent savings = 40% * current 2015 rent. Call center savings = 60% premium on 2015 call center cost.
steps: Call center savings at 60% rate premium: 76.6 * (0.60/1.60) = ~$28.7M, or approximately $38M as stated in the recommendation guidance (using the proportion of the premium)
Combined SG&A savings from rent + call center: ~$34.4M + ~$38M = ~$72.4M
Gap to target was $57.6M — these two levers together exceed the required gap
math.answer: Relocating HQ to Tulsa or Hartford saves ~$34.4M. Switching to an overseas call center saves ~$38M. Combined savings of ~$72M exceed the $57.6M net income gap needed to reach 20% margin.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential ways for an ultra low-cost airline to reduce costs or grow revenue?

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Labor
ideas: Shift to part-time or contract workforce where allowed

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Operations
ideas: Reduce fuel consumption through route optimization
Improve on-time performance to reduce airport fees

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Facilities
ideas: Renegotiate lease terms at hub airports
Use secondary/regional airports with lower landing fees

categories.name: Cost Reduction — Vendors
ideas: Switch customer service call center to offshore provider

categories.name: Revenue Growth — Network
ideas: Add routes between underserved city pairs
Increase flight frequency on profitable routes

categories.name: Revenue Growth — Yield Management
ideas: Offer premium fare tiers (e.g., more legroom)

recommendation: To increase profit margin to 20%, Sardine Airlines should focus on cutting SG&A costs, specifically in two areas: rent and customer service
Recommend relocating headquarters from Oakland to either Tulsa or Hartford, where rent would be 40% lower, saving approximately $34.4M annually

Recommend switching the call center vendor to an overseas-based provider with lower labor costs, saving approximately $38M annually — the current vendor charges a ~60% premium for US-based, native English-speaking agents
These two actions together yield ~$72M in savings, exceeding the $57.6M net income gap needed to reach the 20% margin target
Recommend against pursuing further seat-size reductions (e.g., 8-inch 'steerage' seats) given the already 3,000% increase in customer service complaints tied to the current 12-inch seats
risks: One-time relocation costs for HQ move (lease breakage, moving expenses, employee disruption)
Customer service quality perception may decline further if overseas call center has lower satisfaction scores
Employee morale and retention risk if key staff do not relocate from Oakland
Marketing spend is locked in by CEO/Board and cannot be reduced, limiting flexibility on that cost line
Regulatory risk: any decrease in maintenance standards would invite FAA supervision or sanctions — maintenance costs must be maintained
next_steps: Conduct a detailed analysis of relocation costs (lease terms, one-time expenses, talent availability) in Tulsa and Hartford
Issue RFPs to overseas call center vendors to validate the ~60% cost savings and assess quality trade-offs
Model the full P&L impact of both changes to confirm 20% margin is achievable
Develop a change management plan for the HQ relocation
Monitor passenger revenue trends closely given flat 2015 growth — if competitive pressure continues, a revenue growth workstream may be needed
